title: Vishal Chawla v. Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
coram: Salil Kumar Rai, J. & Mohd. Azhar Husain Idrisi, J.
disposition: Writ dismissed as withdrawn to avail a one-time settlement scheme; compounding, Clause 8.2(vii) and Sections 126 and 135 were not decided
headnote: Vishal Chawla sought a mandamus to permanently disconnect his electricity connection from 1 December 2020 because, he said, he had deposited compounding under Section 152 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The licensee objected that the writ was not maintainable, relying on Division Bench orders, including Bhupendra Singh, that a compounding fee for theft is distinct from liability for unauthorised use under an assessment. The petitioner relied on Executive Engineer v. M/s Sri Seetaram Ricemill (paragraphs 15, 16, 17 and 22) for a distinction between Sections 126 and 135, and on Clause 8.2(vii) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, submitting that acceptance of compounding charges limits further assessment to one time the existing tariff, about Rs. 6.5 lakh, which he was ready to deposit. On 27 October 2023 the Court held only that the matter required consideration, called for a response, and restrained coercive action until the next date if Rs. 6.5 lakh was deposited within a week, subject to the writ. On 4 December 2023 the petition was dismissed as withdrawn, counsel stating that the petitioner wished to avail a departmental one-time scheme for settlement of dues. Maintainability, permanent disconnection, Clause 8.2(vii), and the Sections 126 and 135 point were not decided.
facts:
Vishal Chawla filed Writ-C No. 22278 of 2023 against the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum of Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. and another, seeking a mandamus to permanently disconnect his electricity connection from 1 December 2020 because, he said, compounding under Section 152 of the Electricity Act, 2003 had already been deposited. On 10 October 2023 the compounding order was not on record, and the licensee's counsel was asked to file it.

On 27 October 2023 the licensee objected that a compounding fee for theft is distinct from the assessment for unauthorised use. The petitioner called it a theft case, cited Executive Engineer v. M/s Sri Seetaram Ricemill on Sections 126 and 135, and offered about Rs. 6.5 lakh under Clause 8.2(vii) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 as one time the tariff. The Court called for a reply and, until the next date, restrained coercive steps if that sum was deposited within a week. On 4 December 2023 the writ was dismissed as withdrawn so that he could avail a one-time scheme for settlement of dues.

holding_units.topic: A mandamus for permanent disconnection said to follow deposit of compounding under Section 152 was not decided; the writ was withdrawn
holding_units.question: Does deposit of compounding under Section 152 entitle the consumer to a mandamus for permanent disconnection, and does that deposit end liability for a further assessment?
holding_units.holding: Not decided. The writ sought a mandamus commanding the second respondent to permanently disconnect the petitioner's electricity connection since 1 December 2020 on the ground that compounding contemplated in Section 152 had already been deposited. On 10 October 2023 the Court recorded that the parties had not brought the compounding order on record and directed the licensee's counsel to place it before the next date. On 27 October 2023 the licensee objected to maintainability and relied on Bhupendra Singh, where a Division Bench held that payment of a compounding fee for the offence of theft is altogether distinct from unauthorised use for which the consumer is liable as per assessment, with Sharvan Kumar Jain said to take a similar view and Sandeep Kesarwani also relied on. The Court did not accept or reject that objection. It said the matter required consideration and called for a response. On 4 December 2023 the petition was dismissed as withdrawn so the petitioner could avail a one-time scheme for settlement of dues. Permanent disconnection was not ordered.
holding_units.qualifier: The Section 152 prayer and the maintainability objection are in the order of 27.10.2023 (Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Nand Prabha Shukla, JJ.). The dismissal as withdrawn is the order of 4.12.2023 (Salil Kumar Rai and Mohd. Azhar Husain Idrisi, JJ.) and does not repeat Section 152.

holding_units.topic: The petitioner's one-time-tariff cap under Clause 8.2(vii) was not construed; interim protection was tied to his figure of about Rs. 6.5 lakh, and the writ was then withdrawn
holding_units.question: Where compounding charges are said to have been accepted, does Clause 8.2(vii) limit any further assessment of units to one time the existing tariff?
holding_units.holding: Not decided. The petitioner relied on Clause 8.2(vii): if compounding charges are accepted from the consumer as per the sum prescribed in the Act, any further charges for assessment of units by the licensee shall be at 1.0 times the existing tariff only. He submitted that the amount so computed came to about Rs. 6.5 lakh and that he was ready to deposit it. The Court did not construe Clause 8.2(vii) or find that sum. On 27 October 2023 it said the matter required consideration and, until the next date of listing, directed that no coercive action be taken if the petitioner deposited Rs. 6.5 lakh within a week, subject to the outcome of the writ. The petition was dismissed as withdrawn on 4 December 2023 before any decision on the clause.
holding_units.qualifier: The Clause 8.2(vii) submission and the conditional interim direction are the order of 27.10.2023. The 4.12.2023 withdrawal does not mention the clause or the deposit.
holding_units.paras: order of 27.10.2023, paras 4-5 and 8; order of 4.12.2023, paras 2-3
holding_units.flag: Clause 8.2(vii) is the petitioner's submission, not a construction adopted by the Court. The Rs. 6.5 lakh figure is his computation, which the interim order used as the condition of protection. Whether the deposit was made is not recorded.

holding_units.topic: The petitioner's submission that Sections 126 and 135 are distinct, so that the licensee's authorities did not apply to a theft case, was not decided
holding_units.question: Do Sections 126 and 135 occupy distinct fields, so that authorities treating a compounding fee as distinct from an assessment for unauthorised use do not apply where the consumer's case is one of theft?
holding_units.holding: Not decided. The petitioner relied on paragraphs 15, 16, 17 and 22 of Executive Engineer v. M/s Sri Seetaram Ricemill for a distinction between Sections 126 and 135, and submitted that his case was one of theft, so the judgments cited by the licensee were not attracted. Those paragraphs are not quoted, and the Court did not decide the relationship between the two sections. It said only that the matter required consideration. The writ was later dismissed as withdrawn.
holding_units.qualifier: The submission is paragraph 4 of the order of 27.10.2023. No decision on Sections 126 and 135 appears in the order of 4.12.2023.
holding_units.flag: The judgment names the Supreme Court decision only as 'The Executive Engineer vs. M/s Sri Seetaram Ricemill' and specifies paragraphs 15, 16, 17 and 22. It does not quote them. Sections 126(3) and 126(5) are not cited.

principle_tags.application: The licensee pressed this point for maintainability, through the observation in Bhupendra Singh that a compounding fee for theft is altogether distinct from unauthorised use for which the consumer remains liable as per assessment, with Sharvan Kumar Jain said to be to the same effect. The Court did not adopt the observation. It called for a response, and the writ was dismissed as withdrawn.

authorities.name: Bhupendra Singh @ Bhupendra Singh Chauhan v. State of U.P. and 2 Others
authorities.proposition: Relied on by the licensee for maintainability. As recited, the consumer was found using electricity unauthorisedly, agreed to a compounding fee of Rs. 20,000 to avoid prosecution under Section 135, was provisionally assessed at Rs. 1,27,295, and challenged a demand notice dated 23.05.2019 for both sums on the plea that compounding ended further liability. The Bench observed: 'The argument is completely misconceived inasmuch as payment of compounding fee is in respect of offence of theft is altogether distinct from unauthorized use of electricity for which the petitioner is liable to pay as per assessment.' This Court did not apply that observation.

authorities.proposition: Cited by the petitioner as a judgment of the Supreme Court. Reliance was placed on paragraphs 15, 16, 17 and 22 for a distinction between Sections 126 and 135, and for the submission that the licensee's authorities were not attracted because the case was one of theft. Those paragraphs are not quoted, and this Court did not apply them.
